name: PDF: Communication with Difficult Patients
text: 1 Communication With Difficult Patients Learning Objectives • Identify difficult patients. • Enumerate common triggers that make a patient “difficult” • Summarize issues of dealing with difficult patients. • Enact strategies for working with difficult patients. • Define Motivational Interviewing (MI) • Convey the spirit and principles of MI Some patients have behaviors that make interactions unpleasant, leading to suboptimal outcomes and physician burnout. The ideal patient suffers from an acute, treatable illness and becomes grateful when returned to good health. Any deviation by the patient from this model give a diffic ult patient who may elicit negative reactions from the physician. Difficult patients are defined as those who elicit strong negative emotions from their physicians. If not acknowledged and managed correctly, these feelings can lead to diagnostic errors, unpleasant confrontations, and troublesome complaints or legal claims. What makes a patient “difficult”? 1. Demanding behaviors that necessitate setting realistic limits to the doctor - patient relationship as: • Dependent clingers: those who have an inexhaustible need for love and attention • Manipulative Help -Rejectors: they are pessimistic and have little hope of recovery. These people need and crave attention, yet also fear their need for it. This leads to contradictory behaviour (patients who slash their own wrists, go to hospital, then refuse repair). 2. Stay sick behaviors • Worried Well • Ignoring problems up to self-destructing deny • Noncompliant undermine therapy 3. Resistance to change as resisting lifestyle modifications in diabetic patients. 4. Multiple complaints/problems 2 5. Pain, drug problems • Drug seeking • Chronic pain 6. Psychiatric concerns e,g, borderline PD, substance use disorders and bipolar disorder 7. Difficult diagnoses 8. Others as unfocused patients and slow talkers impeding communication. All these make p atients time-consuming and emotionally draining , convert the communication into a challenging task . In addition, a cultural environment in which every patient can become an “expert” via the Internet has added further challenges. Dealing with difficult patients have several issues that can be summarized into three categories: 1. Doctor-patient relationship- Rapport: Rapport is a harmonious condition in which communication between doctor and patient is effective, and a feeling of mutual understanding exists. Dealing with difficult patients can lead physicians to get out of control , this makes the patient get more and more frustrated. The battle becomes more important than the outcome. Saving face becomes a high priority before solving the problem. At that moment, stepping back can give both the doctor and patient a chance to restart the relationship. 2. Diagnostic Considerations The priority is always to diagnose or to exclude serious conditions. If there is no organic ailment and no intoxication, major psychiatric illness must be considered. • Do not allow your emotions to obscure your judgement. • You should not pass a difficult patient on to a consultant merely as a form of avoidance, but if you've made an honest assessment and still harbour diagnostic doubts, refer. 3 3. Legal Considerations Difficult patients may be angry, hostile, or threatening, and therefore may seek to follow their encounter with letters of complaint or lawsuits. • Try to convince the competent patient to stay until the assessment is complete. Patients are competent to consent or refuse consent if they can fully understand the nature of their problem and the risks or benefits of accepting or rejecting treatment. • If a patient wants to leave against your advice, the patient should be requested to sign a personalized release form that is witnessed. • If the patient refuses to sign a release document, note this refusal on the chart. • "Substituted consent" by a relative is valid only if the patient is incompetent, and the relative clearly acts in the patient's best interest. Allowing a patient to leave or withhold necessary treatment pending consent, and the patient is ill or inflicts harm that was preventable, increases the liability for negligence. Challenging Emotional Conversations with Patients & Families 1. Buster protocol It is used to minimize emotions, so they don’t rule the conversation. • Be prepared • Use non-judgmental listening • Six second rule • Tell me more statements • Empathize and validate • Respond with a wish statement 4 1. Be Prepared • Expect emotions. • Stay calm. • Have a plan for how you will deal. • Monitor what you think and feel • Practice self-regulation – Keep your own emotions in check. • Aim to turn the confrontation into a conversation. • Know when NOT to have conversation (when emotions are too intense). 2. Use Non-Judgmental Listening Remember it’s not about you, but about the other’s disappointments, fears, anxiety and expectations which often underlie the anger, blame or denial on the surface. • Maintain eye contact. • Listen without interrupting, use clarifying statements or paraphrasing. • Avoid trying to make a situation better when it is grave as saying, “I’m sure things will not be as bad as you think.” 3. Six Second Rule: Avoid escalation of conversation. • When your own emotions start to boil in response to anger, wait at least 6 seconds or more to calm down. • Avoid being defensive/blaming e.g. “Well it didn’t work because you waited too long to get help.” • Gather your thoughts and use skills such as “tell me more” or empathic/validating responses. 4. Tell Me More: Invite the person to expand on what they are saying. “Tell me more about your husband.” - “What happened after that?” - “What other concerns do you have?” 5 5. Empathizing and validating to: Acknowledge emotions by empathizing: • “I can see you weren’t expecting this.” • “This isn’t easy to talk about, is it?” • “It’s very stressful, isn’t it?” • “It must be hard to come here every week.” • “I can see how difficult it is for you.” Remember to Avoid phrases such as: “I know how you feel.” - “I feel your pain.” - “It’s going to be alright.” 6. Respond with a wish statement: Let the other person know you hear them and acknowledge that the goal may be desirable, but… • “I wish I didn’t have to tell you this…” • “I wish we had a more effective treatment.” • “I wish things had worked out better.” Important Tip: You entered the room, and t he patient appears impatient • Apologize for the delay while introducing yourself • Sit or stand level with the patient, • make eye contact often, and try not to appear rushed • If tests are required , give realistic estimates of how long they will take Angry patient • Remain calm and verbally comment on what you have observed. • For example: "I see you're angry; can we talk about it?" • I would be upset in your situation too, but let's focus on how I can help you now." 6 Never use excuses with difficult patients Don’t escape by saying "I'm too busy," or "There are no beds." Switch strategies • Sometimes you need to take command, other times, to compromise. • Occasionally humour helps (be careful that you are not misunderstood) You feel yourself becoming angry or frustrated • Do not deny your feelings, try to identify what caused your reaction and formulate a strategy. • Honesty and sincerity will usually be rewarded: tell the patient, "I'm doing my best, but nothing seems to satisfy you," • Find an excuse to leave the bedside for a few minutes before saying something you may regret later. You feel yourself threatened/unsafe End the interaction. • “This conversation is making me feel uncomfortable right now.” • “I don’t feel safe right now and can’t continue this conversation.” 2. Motivational interview (MI) Definition: MI is a collaborative patient-centered directive method for enhancing intrinsic motivation to change by exploring and resolving ambivalence. name: Notes: Pediatric Communication
text: 1 Communication with pediatric patients By Somaya Madkour Prof. of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology 2 Why Do Pediatricians Need Communication Skills? • Pediatricians need communication skills because it is more complicated communicating with children than it is communicating with adults. Children lack the level of comprehension required to properly explain what is happening to them (they are too young to put their problems in words. In other cases, some kids could just be too shy and scared, no matter what age). This is when it falls on the doctors to communicate with them efficiently. • The excitement, fear, and stimulation that comes with a visit to the doctor’s clinic might end up making them too restless, which is not ideal if the child is required to be still for a vaccine shot, or an X-ray. It’s these and more that make communication an important skill in pediatrics. • Because parents and other family members play a crucial role in the lives of children, you need to establish rapport with the family in order to identify mutual goals and facilitate positive outcomes. Communication with children and families Involving the Child in the Conversation The physicians’ approach had to be more child-centered. Invite children to participate in discussions, not only by describing their physical symptoms but also by discussing their feelings and by contributing to decision making. For example, the physician might say to a child, “Lucy, I’m interested in how you feel about what’s going on. Tell me what you think about your upcoming surgery.” Starting the Conversation: Introductions and Opening For an initial visit, make sure you know the patient’s full name before entering the room. Once in the room, check what name the child likes to be called and how adults want to be addressed. Always address the patient and family members by name. Do not address the mother as “Mom” or “Mother” or the father as “Dad” For example, you might say to a child, “Your mother tells me that you’re having some headaches again. Tell me about them.” Introduce yourself. If the patient is a verbally competent child or adolescent, it is appropriate to address him first. “Hello. So, you are Joey (wait for confirmation). Pleased to meet you. I’m Dr. Smith, and (looking at the accompanying adult) who has come with you today?” If the patient is an infant or toddler, you will address the accompanying adult. “Good morning. I’m Doctor Smith, and you are?” The physician will know how the adult wants to be addressed and confirms his relation to the patient. If the accompanying adult doesn’t explain his relation to the patient, ask. If you can, arrange the seating (or choose where to stand if there is no place to sit) so as to face both the patient and the parent. If you must read the patient’s chart or electronic medical record, check laboratory data or read a referral note before taking the history, explain that to the patient. “Just give me a moment to check some data in the computer then we can talk.” You can even invite the patient and parent to look at the computer screen with you. 3 A bit of social chatter or one or two non-medical questions can help put the child and accompanying adult(s) at ease. Then, asking a child why he or she has come to the office or why he or she has been admitted to the hospital can be a helpful starting point, often revealing misconceptions or fears. After introductions and rapport-building, the clinician needs to ask the patient’s and parent’s concerns and reasons for the interview. It is important to let them voice their concerns without interruption, which usually takes less than a minute If there are different concerns that cannot be addressed at this interview, the physician with the patient (if age appropriate) and parent determine which issues will be addressed at this time and which later The Conversation Clinicians working with children need to make a conscious effort to keep children actively involved in discussions about all phases of their care, not just the data gathering phase. Even though young children are not capable of making most medical decisions, they can participate in these decisions and, if given the opportunity, can voice their concerns, their opinions and their preferences. Engaging the child in the conversation in a meaningful way can be a challenge. Children often have more difficulty with open ended questions than do adults, and they often need more time to answer a question than do adults. Give the child time and show that you are comfortable waiting for a response by your verbal language (“It’s okay Eddie, take your time to get your thoughts together.”), by body language (keep your gaze on the child and have a pleasant, patient, expectant look) and by action (don’t look at your watch). Children are likely to be influenced by what their parents have said, and they are likely to give answers they think their parents or the doctor wants. Sometimes you have to encourage the child to voice his or her own thoughts. “That sounds pretty much like what your mother and I said. Are you sure that you agree? What would you like to do differently?” Closing the Conversation There are three important components for effective closure of a patient interview 1- Summarizing at the end of a clinical interview is primarily a technique to be sure that the family understands how you see the situation. 2- Explaining the Plan Explaining what is going to happen next helps the patient cope with the illness. A yes answer to, “Do you understand?” is not a reliable indicator of comprehension. Many patients are embarrassed to admit that they don’t understand or think they understand when they do not. The question, “Is there something that I haven’t made clear or something that you would like me to clarify?” is stronger encouragement for the child or parent to ask for clarification 3- Soliciting Questions The typical, “Any questions?” delivered while standing up and moving towards the door is not the most effective incentive. Asking, “What questions do you have?” while remaining seated is more likely to elicit a meaningful response. If you sense that the patient or parent is confused, you can ask, “You look to me to be a bit uncertain. What can I clarify or go over again?” This is less intimidating than, “What don’t you understand? 4 Techniques to Facilitate Communication Touch Infants do not have cognitive understanding of the words they hear, but they sense the emotional support, and they can feel, interpret, and respond to gentle, loving, supportive hands caring for them. School-age children and adolescents appreciate giving and receiving hugs and getting a reassuring pat on the back or a gentle hand on the hand. The physician, however, needs to request permission for any contact beyond a casual touch with these children. Physical Proximity and Environment Creating a supportive, inviting environment for children includes the use of child -size furniture, colorful banners and posters, developmentally appropriate toys, and art displayed at a child’s eye level. This is essential to overcome feeling of anxiety being in unfamiliar environment. You can also keep comic books, workbooks, and balls to engage older children in a similar way. Once they’re in the examination room, ensure you engage them in conversation about the games and puzzles. Their anxiety is likely to increase once they’re out of the waiting room, so keeping them distracted and entertained is important. On your part, ensure all the toys are properly sanitized to reduce the risk of infections. Listening By practicing active listening skills, physician can be effective listeners. Active listening skills are as follows: Attentiveness Eliminating distractions whenever possible is important. For example, the physician should maintain eye contact, close the room door, and eliminate potential distractions (e.g., television, computer, video games, smartphones). Clarification through Reflection Refl

name: PDF: communication with elderly patient
text: 1 Communication with elderly patients By Somaya Madkour Prof. of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology 2 Communication with elderly patients The aging process can cause changes in physical, cognitive, and social aspects. Some seniors may experience memory problems, speech difficulties, or hearing difficulties. These factors can affect their ability to communicate effectively. In addition to physical challenges, older adults may also face feelings of loneliness, social isolation, or feelings of being unappreciated. Therefore, a communication approach that acknowledges and respects their feelings is very important to create meaningful relationships and help the elderly feel heard and cared for. it is important to avoid paternalistic attitudes that might limit their participation in making decisions about their own health. Instead, the role of the health professional is to be a good listener, respect older people's perspectives, and seek a deeper understanding of their needs and preferences. This can help create a more inclusive and empathetic environment, which in turn will improve the quality of care and satisfaction of the elderly with the services provided Empathy and patience Listening. Good listening skills will help create a trusting relationship and will greatly benefit the care and well - being of the elderly. Trusting environment is essential for collaboration in treatment and following medical instructions. The elderly often experience hearing loss or certain cognitive problems. Listening with empathy and patience gives older people time to process information and respond better. Reflection is the skill to repeat or conclude what the elderly have said. By using reflection, you show that you are really listening and understanding what they are saying. This helps validate their feelings and experiences and creates a stronger emotional bond. A physician recently saw an elderly patient with parkinsonism and depression. The patient began by noting that he had numerous bad experiences with physician and health care system. The physician listened attentively and used rapport building skills in the initial 5 minutes. Although the patient had numerous criticisms of other physicians, the interviewer did not have to join in this criticism to build rapport. Empathetic communication is sufficient it seems like you have had some troubling experiences with the medical system ( reflection) I can understand how you felt insignificant and unimportant ( legitimation) 3 I want you to know that I care about your difficulties and I will do my best to work with you to develop a plan to bring you some relief ( support and partnership) Simple language and easy to understand. The elderly often have difficulty understanding complex or technical language, especially if they have cognitive decline or hearing loss. By using simple language, older people are more likely to understand messages better and feel more confident in dealing with care and treatment. Also it easier for them to understand the treatment options available, the risks and benefits and allows them to participate actively in making decisions about their own health. Simple and clear language helps reduce the risk of misunderstandings and ensures that the information conveyed is received correctly. Use different learning techniques to ensure understanding: visual aids including pictures , audiovisual, computers programmers and diagrams can be used with written and verbal instructions to enhance understanding Create a comfortable environment A comfortable physical and social environment is very important in communicating with the elderly. Avoid noisy or crowded environments. Loud and excessive noise can distract the elderly and make it difficult for them to concentrate or listen properly. Make sure the room has enough lighting so that your face and body movements are clearly visible. Adequate lighting will help seniors see your facial expressions and body language, which are important in communication. Make sure that the chairs and other facilities in the room are comfortable for the elderly. Show a friendly, caring, and polite attitude when communicating with the elderly. Greet them with a smile and speak in a gentle tone of voice to let them feel more relaxed and open to talking. It is important to respect the privacy of the elderly and provide opportunities for them to speak without pressure. Speak attentively and don't force personal questions if the elderly don't want to talk about it. Open questions Asking open-ended questions and using the skills of reflection, legitimation, support, partnership and respect are especially useful when interacting with older adults. Open questions are questions that require the elderly to provide more detailed and in-depth answers than just "yes" or "no". The elderly often have complex feelings and emotions related to health problems and changes that occur to them. By asking open-ended questions, you give them the opportunity to express their emotions more freely and openly. This can help them deal with any feelings of stress, anxiety, or loneliness they may be experiencing. Open-ended questions allow you to get more information about older people's health problems or needs. You can better understand what is most important to them in care and how you can help meet those needs. 4 Also use facilitation, surveying and clarification It is essential to do checking or summarization because of hearing, vision, cognitive and communication difficulties, elderly patient may not succeed in transmitting information accurately to the physician the first time. also checking information helps to confirm the reliability of information physician : with so much going on your life, let me repeat back what I have just heard to make sure I have understood your problem correctly if a family member or caregiver is present physician: I have spent some time with your ( spouse, father…) please let me know how you think he or she has been doing Respect for autonomy and participation Respecting the autonomy of the elderly and giving them the opportunity to participate in making decisions about their care are important aspects of communication with the elderly. This helps to make them feel confident, valued and have an active role in their health care. Older adults who are involved in making decisions about their care tend to have a better understanding of information about their health conditions and available treatment options. They will ask more questions, seek information, and consider all options better, which can ultimately lead to more informed treatment decisions that match their preferences. Convey realistic expectations Reliability and honesty in conveying information about health conditions and prognosis are important principles in communication with the elderly. Honesty and accuracy in providing information help build trust between the elderly and medical personnel. By conveying clear and realistic information about health conditions, the elderly and their families can make appropriate preparations and plan treatment better. Giving false hope to the elderly will only cause disappointment if these expectations are not met. Hiding or withholding important information does not respect their rights to get a clear and complete explanation about their health. Overcome feelings of loneliness and isolation The elderly often experience feelings of loneliness and social isolation, especially if they have physical or mobility limitations that limit social interaction. Effective communication provides an opportunity for older people to talk and interact with others, especially if they are living in a care facility or facing social isolation. These interactions can provide a sense of social connection and reduce feelings of loneliness. text: 1 Communication with patients with special needs By Somaya Madkour Prof. of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology 2 Communication with patient with special needs In medical practice we encounter patients of all backgrounds who may have disabilities. These populations have a wide range of cognitive, expressive , receptive and physical capacities. So, it is important for healthcare providers to be aware of these challenges and to adapt their communication style accordingly. Communication Challenges Faced by Patients with Special Needs • Speech or language disorders: They may have difficulty articulating words or understanding spoken language. • Hearing or vision impairments: They may have difficulty communicating with others if they cannot see or hear what is being said. • Cognitive disabilities: They may have difficulty understanding complex medical information or making decisions about their care. • Mental health conditions: They may have difficulty communicating their thoughts and feelings. • Cultural or linguistic barriers: People who speak a different language or come from a different culture may have difficulty communicating with their healthcare providers. These healthcare communication barriers can be due to language barriers, cultural differences in communication styles, or lack of familiarity with the healthcare system. In all of these conditions it difficult to communicate their needs and preferences to their healthcare providers. Cognitive disabilities Common examples of patients with cognitive disabilities include those with: • Down syndrome • autism spectrum disorders • mental disorders. Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Intellectual, Cognitive or Developmental Disabilities • Treat adults with intellectual, cognitive or developmental disabilities as adults. • Adjust your method of communication as necessary depending on the individual's responses to you. Use simple, direct sentences or supplementary visual forms of communication, such as gestures, diagrams, or demonstrations, if indicated. • Use concrete, specific language. Avoid abstract language and simplistic wording. When possible, use words that relate to things you both can see. Avoid using directional terms such as right, left, east, or west. • Be prepared to repeat the same information more than once in different ways. 3 • When asking questions, phrase them without suggesting desired or preferred responses as some people with intellectual, cognitive or developmental disabilities may tell you what they think you want to hear. • Give exact instructions. For example, “You will see the nurse at 10:30,” rather than “Come back to see the nurse in 15 minutes.” • Avoid giving too many directions at one time, which may be confusing. Eliminate distractions and minimize background noise if possible. • Avoid sensory overload by providing information gradually and clearly. • Provide information in written or verbal form if that is the person’s preference. • Recognize that the person may need to have directions repeated and may take notes to help remember directions or the sequence of tasks. He or she may also benefit from watching a task demonstrated. • Do not pretend to understand if you do not. Ask the person to repeat what was said. Be patient, flexible, and supportive. • Do not assume that the person will be able to read well; some may not read at all. • Be respectful, kind, and don’t talk down to them or their loved ones. Maintain eye contact and a welcoming demeanor that invites communication. Understand there may be a healthy fear of healthcare personnel. We must maintain an open dialogue and convey that the patient’s thoughts, ideas, and concerns are important and welcome. Down syndrome can result in a broad range of mild, moderate, or severe cognitive and physical delays Each patient is unique in his abilities and limitations, and care should be tailored to individual needs. When providing care for a patient with Down syndrome, tailor care to the patient’s developmental age rather than his or her actual age. Talk to the patient’s caregivers and ask questions so you can understand where your patient is developmentally. A 30-year-old male patient with Down syndrome is admitted to your unit. He’s articulate and appears to be very high functioning. His caregiver is at the business office addressing his insurance information while you begin your assessment. As you’re asking the patient questions, you realize that he has some learning deficits that are impeding the interview. You wait for the caregiver to return so you can collaborate on the admission forms and health history. You involve the patient in every step and formulate questions to his cognitive needs as possible 4 Patients with an autism spectrum disorder can present a challenge. Many children and adults with autism spectrum disorders have difficulty communicating with words that they’re becoming frustrated, anxious, or uncomfortable. They may begin humming, pacing, or yelling. Consult with the patient’s family or caregiver to find out what historically has worked to calm the patient down. Common nonpharmacologic interventions, such as decreasing environmental stimuli by reducing noise and distractions (such as the TV), can often greatly reduce the patient’s anxiety. Having the family provide familiar items may also reduce anxiety. It’s best to have the same healthcare provider care for the patient during each visit because patients with autism spectrum disorders do better with comfortable routines, and familiar faces and places. You’re working in the ED of a busy Level-1 trauma facility when a 17-year-old patient with an autism spectrum disorder arrives. He presents with tachycardia and is growing increasingly anxious. His parents state that the patient doesn’ t like the hemodynamic alarms that are audible in the distance. He’ s having great difficulty communicating his abdominal pain symptoms and begins rapidly rocking back and forth in his chair. You consider that the patient is experiencing too much environmental stimuli, contributing to his anxiety. You move the patient to an area that has decreased environmental stimuli to help calm him so you can proceed with your physical assessment. Ask the patient and his or her caregiver about activities of daily living routines to minimize anxiety and frustration. As with Down syndrome, make no assumptions regarding the patient’s intelligence, level of understanding, or ability. Ask the patient and his or her caregiver for input and assistance in determining approach, language, and needs assessment. Many patients experience mental disorders, such as paranoid schizophrenia, clinical depression, and bipolar disorder. These disorders can impact the patient’s quality of life, causing unusual shifts in mood, energy, and activity levels, and affecting the ability to carry out daily tasks and engage in social or occupational activities that he once enjoyed Recommendations for Communicating with Patients with Psychiatric/Mental Health Disabilities 5 • Approach the person as you would anyone else; speak directly to the person, using clear, simple communication. • Treat persons who are adults as adults. Use the same good manners in interacting with a person who has a psychiatric/mental health disability that you would with anyone else. • Do not make decisions for the person or assume that you know the person’s preferences. • Offer to shake hands when introduced. • Make eye contact, and be aware of your own body language. Like others, people with psychiatric/mental health disabilities will sense your discomfort. • Listen attentively, and wait for the person to finish speaking. If needed, clarify what the person has said. • Use concrete terms and avoid vague or generalized descriptions. • Although there are similar signs and symptoms with some mental disorders, remember that no two patients are alike. text: 1 Physician responsibilities towards community Intended Learning Outcomes: By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: 1. Describe the key responsibilities of physicians towards their communities. 2. Explain the importance of public health and preventive medicine. 3. Discuss the ethical obligations to engage in disaster management. 4. Identify physician’s role in response to violence and abuse. 5. Define the E. professionalism. 6. Discuss ethical conduct when sharing medical content on media. 7. Define competency and explain how a physician could fulfill it. Physicians' primary ethical obligation to individual patients is to diagnose and treat illnesses through using their expertise, ensure patients receive the best possible care plus educate patients about their conditions and treatments to make informed decisions about their health. However, they also have a responsibility towards the whole community. They participate in activities to protect and promote the health of the public and to protect public safety. Key responsibilities of physicians towards their communities: 1. Public Health and Preventive Medicine: Besides focusing on diagnosis and treatment, physicians also have a professional commitment to promote public health. Public health focuses on protecting and improving the health of populations through education, policymaking, screening and researching for disease and injury prevention . Examples include: a. Preventive Care: It is the application of healthcare measures to prevent diseases. Physicians should: • Be updated about preventive care guidelines that are well supported by the best available evidence. • Recommend and encourage patients to have appropriate vaccinations and screenings. 2 b. Screening and reporting infectious diseases: To protect the interests of individual patients and fulfill the public health obligations in the context of viral infections as HBV , HCV , HIV , physicians should: • Support routine, universal screening for infectious diseases as HBV , HCV , HIV . • Respect for autonomy by respecting a patient’s informed decision to perform screening tests. • Test patients without prior consent only in limited cases in which harm to third parties may occur as testing to protect occupationally exposed health care professionals or patients. • Ensure that patients who tested positive receive appropriate follow-up care. • Report the specific authority and notify the endangered third party. • Safeguard the confidentiality of patient information to the greatest extent possible when reporting. c. Injury prevention from impaired drivers: Certain medical condition may impair driving abilities causing threats to both public safety and patient’s own well-being. To serve the interests of patients and the public, physicians should: • Assess at-risk patients for conditions adversely affect their driving ability. • If physicians are not able to evaluate the effect of medical condition, refer at- risk patient for assessment • Help the patient through options for treatment or therapy if available. • Prior to reporting, explain to the patient that you have an obligation to report a medically at -risk driver as continuing to drive poses a clear risk to public safety. d. Routine universal immunization of physicians: Physicians have an ethical responsibility to encourage patients to accept immunization. They also have to take appropriate measures in their own practice to prevent the spread of infectious disease in health care settings. Regarding highly transmissible diseases, that pose significant medical risk for vulnerable patients, and 3 for which there is an available, safe, and effective vaccine, physicians have a responsibility to accept immunization if there is no contraindication. 2. Health promotion and education: Health promotion should be a collaborative, patient -centered process that includes educating and motivating patients regarding healthy lifestyle, helping patients by assessing their needs, preferences, and readiness for change. Physicians should: • Participate in public health campaigns, workshops or seminars to raise awareness about important health issues such as smoking cessation, nutrition, and mental health. • Educate patients about relevant modifiable risk factors. • Promote training in health promotion during medical school. • Support research to improve the evidence for health promotion. 3. Physicians’ Responsibilities in Disaster Response & Preparedness: Responses to national, regional or local disasters require extensive involvement from physicians to provide urgent medical care. This obligation may carry risks to physicians’ own safety, health, or life. Therefore, besides their routine professional duties, doctors also must protect themselves and their own families from harm. Physician should: • Maintaining the patients’ interests. • Treating patients with equal respect, compassion and dignity. • Respecting patient autonomy, privacy and confidentiality as possible. • Treating patients’ family members with respect as they also need support. • Advocating for accountability, fairness, equity and justice in the provision of health care and the allocation of health care resources. • Advocating for accountability, fairness, equity and justice in the treatment of the health care workforce and the safety of the health care environment. • Working collaboratively and supporting colleagues and other health care professionals during and after a disaster. 4 • Looking after one’s own health and well-being in order to be able to care for others. 4. Identifying, treating and reporting violence & Abuse: Physicians have an ethical obligation to take appropriate action to avert the harm caused by violence and abuse. Physicians should be familiar with: • How to detect and response to violence or abuse. • Community and health resources that are available to abused persons. • Public health measures that are effective in preventing violence and abuse. • Legal requirements for reporting violence or abuse. Moreover, physician should: • Raise public awareness about the problem of abuse, violence and domestic violence. • Consider abuse as a possible factor in the medical complaints. • Identify signs of abuse to reduce the volume of unidentified cases. • Treat the immediate symptoms and sequelae of violence and abuse. • Provide ongoing care to address long-term consequences of violence. • Discuss any suspicion of abuse sensitively with the patient. • Report suspected violence and abuse after informing patients about requirements to report. • Protect patient privacy by disclosing only the minimum necessary information. In addition, physicians should not be influenced by misconceptions about abuse, including beliefs that it is rare, does not occur in “normal” families, and is a private matter best resolved without outside interference, or is caused by victims’ own actions. 5. Reporting of Adverse Events Post marketing, cases in which there is a causal relationship between use of a drug and an adverse event, especially a serious event, may be rare. A physician who 5 suspects that an adverse reaction to a drug or medical device has occurred, whatever its severity, has an ethical responsibility to manage these adverse events and to communicate that information to the professional community through established reporting mechanisms. 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: Physicians involved in the media environment should be aware of their ethical obligations to patients, the public, and the medical profession; and that their conduct can affect their medical colleagues, other health care professionals, as well as institutions with which they are affiliated. Media includes both the traditional media (radio and TV) and the new social media platforms. E-Professionalism is the professional use of electronic platforms. It includes online attitudes, actions, and adherence to relevant professional codes of conduct and princi

name: PDF: intra-interprof
text: 1 Interprofessional & Intraprofessional Relationships in Healthcare By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Define Interprofessional and Intraprofessional Relationships 2. Identify competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration 3. Demonstrate effective communication Strategies for collaborating with other healthcare professionals. 4. Discuss Common Barriers to effective professional communication 5. Explain Intra/Interprofessional significance in healthcare settings. 6. Analyze Ethical Issues in Interprofessional Relationships Definitions: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), interprofessional collaboration occurs when “multiple health workers from different professional backgrounds work together with patients, families, caregivers and communities to deliver the highest quality of care across settings.” E.g. collaboration between physicians, nurses, pharmacists, physical therapists and the social care profession. Regarding the intraprofessional relationship, it is the collaboration between two or more disciplines within the same profession e.g. collaboration between a pediatrician and neurosurgeon for the sake of the patient. Competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration: Competencies identified for intra/interprofessional collaboration are categorized into six domains: 1. Patient-centered care 2. Interprofessional communication 3. Participatory leadership 4. Conflict resolution 5. Transparency of duties and responsibilities 6. Teamwork 2 1. Patient-centered care: Patient-centered care is one of the main competencies in the healthcare system. It ensures the safety and quality of healthcare. Patient-centered care is the degree to which patients and their families are satisfied with their care and involved in decision making process and to which those providing the care do so with sensitivity and respect for the patient’s need, expectations and individual differences. One of the dimensions of patient-centered care is the coordination and smooth transition from one healthcare setting to another. 2. Intra/ interprofessional communication: It describes the sharing of information (by means of verbal, writing or other medium) among members of different health professionals’ fields in a responsive and responsible manner that supports a team and influence patient care positively. Components of Intra/ Interprofessional Communication • Effective communication tools, information systems and communication technologies that facilitate interactions. • Avoiding discipline-specific terminology when communicating information with patients, families, community members. • Expressing one’s knowledge and opinions to team members with clarity, and respect to ensure common understanding of information. • Active listening to encourage ideas and opinions of other team members. • Giving sensitive, constructive feedback to others about their performance on the team. • Using respectful language in difficult situations, or during conflict. General Barriers to Intra/ Interprofessional Communication: • Personal values and expectations and personality differences • Organizational hierarchy • Varying team members who may not have worked together before • Cultural diversity and generational differences • Historical interprofessional and intraprofessional competitions 3 • Differences in language and medical jargon • Differences in schedules and professional routines • Varying levels of preparation, qualifications, and status • Fears of diluted professional identity • Diverse clinical responsibilities • Increased complexity of patient care • Emphasis on rapid decision-making ISBARR communication model: A common format used by health care team members to exchange client information is ISBARR, a mnemonic for the components of Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Request/Recommendations, and Repeat back. • Introduction: Introduce your name, role, and the agency from which you are calling. • Situation: Provide the patient’s name and location, the reason you are calling, recent vital signs, and the status of the patient. • Background: Provide background information about the patient such as admission date and diagnosis, current condition , recent relevant lab or diagnostic results, previous illnesses and allergies. • Assessment: Share abnormal assessment findings and your evaluation of the current situation. • Request/Recommendations: such as reassessment, order a lab/diagnostic test, prescribe/change medication. • Repeat back: to confirm accuracy. Be sure to document communication in the patient’s chart. 3. Participatory leadership: It is a unique leadership style, also referred to as democratic leadership. Participative leaders recognize the significant role of all members in team success, so they encourage all team members to provide feedback and participate in shared decision-making. They also promote transparent communication and collaborative solutions. 4 4. Conflict resolution: It happens when healthcare providers work as a team that actively engages in addressing disagreements and responding effectively to all types of conflict . To support interprofessional practice, health providers should: • create a safe environment where differing opinions are welcome • validate and acknowledge differing perspectives • communicate positively and constructively • see conflict with the potential for a positive outcome 5. Teamwork: A multidisciplinary team is a group of individuals from different professional backgrounds, each bringing their own specialized expertise to work together on a common goal which is achieving patient-centered care. 6. Transparency of duties and responsibilities: This competence helps all team members to understand their own and others' roles and duties and use one another's knowledge and skills to perform the right task. Significance of Inter/Intra professional relation in healthcare settings: Both are increasingly recognized as important due to the complex and dynamic nature of healthcare organizations and the growing specialization of healthcare professions. They are essential to: 1. Enhances patient care and outcomes When healthcare professionals work together, they can provide comprehensive and well-coordinated care by ensuring that all aspects of a patient’s condition are addressed, leading to more accurate diagnoses and treatment plans. 2. Mitigates medical errors According to the Joint Commission, miscommunication during patient handoffs contributes to an estimated 80% of serious medical errors. By working together, 5 healthcare providers can identify and address potential safety issues more effectively regarding medication management, patient handoffs, and care transitions, which are critical points for errors. 3. Expedites initiation of treatment A substantial proportion of healthcare is marked by waiting periods. Patients await physician consultations and physicians await input from other interprofessional team members. Communication delays allow medical conditions to deteriorate. A clinical collaboration platform efficiently delivers pertinent information to the right individuals at the right time via secure messaging, voice, or video leading to a better quality of care. 4. Diminishes inefficiencies and healthcare costs Interprofessional collaboration ensures more efficient resource utilization, leading to cost savings and improved resource allocation. For example, when a team of professionals collaborates on a patient’s care plan, unnecessary tests and procedures and duplicated work can be avoided, reducing both the financial burden on patients and the strain on healthcare facilities. 5. Advances staff relations and job satisfaction Optimizing clinical workflows through improved interdisciplinary collaboration helps reduce burnout and improve clinician satisfaction. On the contrary, poor intra- and interprofessional teamwork is associated with higher rates of inadequate or missed care, medical errors

Seeks to identify situations or factors likely to give rise to human error and change the underlying systems of care in order to reduce the occurrence of errors or minimize their impact on patients. Example 1: Home Medications Contribute to a Unique Opportunity for Error on Discharge from the Hospital. Audit M easuring a clinical outcome or a process, against well-defined standards set on the principles of evidence-based medicine. E.g. Tracer method LOs Understand the concepts and principles of patient safety and how they apply to clinical practice. Identify the common causes and consequences of patient harm and how to prevent and manage them. Recognize the role and responsibilities of health care professionals in ensuring patient safety and promoting a culture of safety. Apply evidence-based strategies and tools to improve patient safety and quality of care. Root Cause Analysis (RCA) Root cause analysis (RCA) is the process of discovering the root causes of problems in order to identify appropriate solutions. RCA assumes that it is much more effective to systematically prevent and solve for underlying issues rather than just treating ad hoc symptoms and putting out fires. Techniques: 5 Whys Change/event analysis Fishbone diagram Checklists FMEA Summary To err is human Error in medicine leads to catastrophe To safeguard against errors, a strong system should be designed (systems approach) to put barriers in the way of errors causing damage ( swiss cheese model) Methods applied in patient safety are: Incident reporting Change/event analysis RCA Audits FMEA Thank you Stay safe Definitions Patient safety: A voiding harm to patients from care that is intended to help them. Near-miss Error Adverse events Preventable Ameliorable Due to negligence High Reliability Organizations (HROs) “…catastrophic safety failures are almost never caused by isolated errors committed by individuals. Instead, most accidents result from multiple, smaller errors in environments that have serious underlying system flaws…”

text: Lecture slides Professional safety Ahmed Elsheshai MD MRCPsych Psychiatrist standard precautions: hand washing, respiratory hygiene, safe collection and disposal of health-care waste, and environmental hygiene Use safety-engineered devices and follow good practices for safe injections Ensure adequate ventilation in all indoor health-care settings Provide immunization at no cost to health workers BCG HBV polio pertussis diphtheria measles rubella meningococcal influenza varicella COVID-19 cholera Use of ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) for disinfection and prevention of airborne pathogens Use clinical triage for early identification of patients with respiratory infections to prevent transmission Ensure adequate supply, proper use and maintenance of well fitted PPE II. Ergonomic risk Up to 72% of nurses are suffering from non-specific chronic low back pain. Low back pain is associated with health workers’ absenteeism, reduced efficiency, increased economic burden, decreased quality of life, and burnout. Preventive measures Avoid lifting or use fewer and more efficient lifting operations Plan tasks carefully to reduce ergonomic stress and strains Use lifting aids and mechanical devices for patient handling to prevent unnecessary lifting In absence of lifting aids, ensure that at least two workers lift the patient Provide training on safe patient handling Adjust the layout of working areas to ensure enough space for safe transfers LOs Explain the importance of occupational health and safety for health workers Identify the most common occupational risks to health and safety that health workers face, such as infection, fatigue, injury, violence, and mental health problems Describe the rights and responsibilities of health workers and employers regarding decent working conditions and protection from harm Apply measures for preventing and managing workplace violence, such as recognizing warning signs, communicating effectively, and using teamwork skills Access and use supportive services and resources for protecting and improving the health and well-being of health workers Plan tasks carefully to reduce ergonomic stress and strains Use lifting aids and mechanical devices for patient handling to prevent unnecessary lifting In absence of lifting aids, ensure that at least two workers lift the patient Adjust the layout of working areas to ensure enough space for safe transfers III. Chemical risk Acute risks: Asphyxiation Acid burns Dizziness Nausea Vomiting Chronic risks: Asthma Bronchitis Dermatitis Cancer Liver damage Most common culprits Disinfectants cleaning products sterilants anesthetic gases mercury hazardous drugs pesticides Preventive measures Eliminate unnecessary chemicals or substitute with equally effective and less toxic chemicals Ensure adequate ventilation and use of closed systems when handling chemicals Provide medical surveillance and regular training for workers handling chemicals Apply safe work procedures for handling, storage, transportation and disposal of all chemicals according to the recommendations of the manufacturer Provide facilities for personal hygiene including washing and changing clothes Ensure safe disposal of empty or nearly empty pesticides containers Organize first aid and emergency care procedures in case of accidental exposures Provide and ensure usage of appropriate well fitted PPE IV. Radiation hazard Ionizing radiation (X-ray & CT) may cause: skin and blood damage Cataract Infertility Birth defects Cancer UV radiation (phototherapy, germicidal lamps) can cause: Skin cancer, Skin burn and Cataract, while Lasers (scalpel, diathermy, hair removal) can cause: Tissue burns, Eye damage, Fire and explosion and system failures (1). Protective measures Use radiation only to cases where the benefits outweigh the risks Put in place shielding, protective barriers , safety interlocks, warning signs and signals Obtain permission from the relevant authority for medical use of radiation and follow the recommendations for safe use Restrict access to areas where radiation is used to authorized persons only Train workers on safe use of equipment and sources of radiation Organize regular inspection of medical radiation devices by the competent authority Monitor exposure and organize medical surveillance of exposed workers Encourage female workers to report if they become pregnant and reallocate them to tasks without radiation exposure Develop standard operating procedures for action in case of accidental exposure to radiation Report all accidental and planned exposures above the exposure limit Provide workers with adequate PPE including protective aprons, gloves and organ shields Follow the measures recommended by the manufactures for use of medical devices with non-ionizing radiation (UV & lasers) Why? Put in place shielding, protective barriers , safety interlocks, warning signs and signals Restrict access to areas where radiation is used to authorized persons only Monitor exposure and organize medical surveillance of exposed workers Provide workers with adequate PPE including protective aprons, gloves and organ shields V. Psychosocial risks Intrinsic demands of the job, individual susceptibility, and poor work organization contributes to increased stress in health workers. Role conflict Lack of autonomy Prolonged job stress may cause burnout, chronic fatigue, absenteeism, high staff turnover, reduced patient satisfaction, and increased diagnosis and treatment errors. Preventive measures Organizational interventions: to respect, plan for, and accommodate stressful environment and stressed staff Training Managers: to spot signs of stress in employees Employees: higher mental health literacy Individual interventions: CBT, mindfulness, stress coping skills, self care, physical activity Evidence-based mental health clinical care Organize work to reduce job strain: optimizing workload and working time ensuring safe staffing levels encouraging regular breaks having flexible schedules Optimize shift lengths Provide accommodation for health workers VI. Violence and harassment Violence and harassment affect all health worker groups and work settings in the health sector. Up to 62% of health workers have experienced workplace violence. Verbal abuse (58%) is the most common form of non-physical violence, followed by threats (33%) and sexual harassment (12%). Ourselves Our loved ones Our patients The community at large Resources Identify risks of violence Improve work organization Optimal staffing levels, working time, supportive work teams and improved working conditions Prevent staff from working alone and minimize patient waiting time Provide timely information to patients and family to reduce stress Restrict movement of the public in health facilities Security measures Train workers in conflict resolution and managing assaults Provide counselling to recognize the danger of violent behaviour and assistance to change the conduct/attitude Maintain physical fitness and emotionally stable psychical conditions Respond quickly and appropriately to incidents if they occur Encourage reporting, recording and monitoring of all incidents Ensure a confidential complaint or grievance procedure Monitor violence trends and the effectiveness of preventive measures VII. Working outdoors in situations of extreme cold or heat can cause serious health damage. Poor lighting in work areas can cause injuries, eye strain and loss of vision. name: Privilege and discrimination
text: Lecture slides Privilege , discrimination, & diversity Ahmed Elsheshai MD MRCPsych Exercise Privilege This is our country, we have a stronger claim to jobs even if we are more lazy, incompetent, or more expensive. Stereotype Immigrants are bad people expelled from their countries Prejudice immigrants are the reason for our economic difficulty Institutional power Passing a law to prioritize natives in job interviews Oppression Deporting immigrants and separating them from their children 4 levels of oppression Personal: values, beliefs, feelings. Interpersonal: actions, behaviors, language. Institutional: rules, policies, procedures. Cultural: beauty, truth, right. Targets of oppression Members of social identity groups that are disenfranchised, exploited, and victimized by agents of oppression and the agent’s systems or institutions. Subject to containment, having their choices and movements restricted and limited. Are seen and treated as expendable and replaceable. without an individual identity apart from their group. compartmentalized into narrowly defined roles. Kept in their place by the agent of oppression’s ideology. Fewer “life chances” or benefits as a result of their membership in a particular social group. Agents of oppression Members of the dominant social groups. Privileged by birth or acquisition, which knowingly or unknowingly exploit and reap unfair advantage over members of groups that are targets of oppression. Agents of oppression are also trapped by the system of institutionalized oppression that benefits them and are confined to roles and prescribed behaviors. Internalized oppression The process whereby people in the target group make oppression internal and personal by coming to believe that the lies, prejudices, and stereotypes about them are true. Members of target groups exhibit internalized oppression when they alter their attitudes, behaviors, speech, and self-confidence to reflect the stereotypes and norms of the dominant group. Internalized oppression can create low self-esteem, self-doubt, and even self-loathing. It can also be projected outward as fear, criticism, and distrust of members of one’s target group. Ally A person whose commitment to dismantling oppression is reflected in a willingness to do the following: Educate oneself about oppression; Learn from and listen to people who are targets of oppression; Examine and challenge one’s own prejudices, stereotypes, and assumptions; Work through feelings of guilt, shame, and defensiveness to understand what is beneath them and what needs to be healed; Learn and practice the skills of challenging oppressive remarks, behaviors, policies, and institutional structures; Act collaboratively with members of the target group to dismantle oppression. Exercise All that is said in the group is confidential and will be respected. No one will be asked to reflect unless they want to do so. Nothing that is said in the group will be shared beyond the group experience. It is ok to disagree, yet we must disagree with kindness and a desire to understand the other person point of view. Allow others to finish their comments before speaking. Thank you LOs Define the concept of privilege Reflect on the impact of privilege on one’s own life Compare the effects of implicit bias and privilege Identify the effect of privilege on health equity Consider ways to honestly address privilege in systems Sarah and Ahmed are both highly qualified employees at a company. They have similar job roles, years of experience, and performance records. Recently, a management position opened, and both Sarah and Ahmed applied for the promotion. The company is based in the UK, Sarah is British and Ahmed is an immigrant. The company is a nursery, and the position is head teacher. Hala and Hassan both work at a large financial firm. They were hired around the same time, have similar qualifications, and have consistently received positive performance reviews. However, their career trajectories have been quite different. Hala, who is from a privileged background and attended an elite university, has quickly moved up the corporate ladder. She has been given numerous opportunities for leadership roles and prestigious projects. Hassan, who comes from a less privileged background and attended a state university, has found it challenging to secure promotions and high-profile assignments despite his hard work and competence. He has also faced subtle biases and microaggressions from some colleagues. Hala is promoted to a senior management position, while Hassan continues to work in his current role with no clear path for advancement. Privilege Privilege operates on personal, interpersonal, cultural, and institutional levels… and gives advantages, favors, and benefits… to members of dominant groups… at the expense of members of target groups. Stereotype An exaggerated or distorted belief that attributes characteristics to members of a particular group, simplistically lumping them together and refusing to acknowledge differences among members of the group. E.g. Women are bad drivers; Chinese are good at math. Prejudice A judgment or opinion that is formed on insufficient grounds before facts are known or in disregard of facts that contradict it. Prejudices are learned and can be unlearned. E.g. a car coming out of a parking spot hits the car next to it, who do you think is driving? Institutional power The ability or official authority to decide what is best for others. The ability to decide who will have access to resources. The capacity to exercise control over others. Oppression The combination of prejudice and institutional power which creates a system that discriminates against some groups (often called “target groups”) and benefits other groups (often called “dominant groups”). Examples: racism, sexism, ableism, classism, and ageism. These systems enable dominant groups to exert control over target groups by limiting their rights, freedom, and access to basic resources such as health care, education, employment, and housing. E.g. women are forbidden from driving
